title: Loving Jesus above all (II.7)
hook: love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself
tomorrow: can you be close friends with someone you can't see?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two wings: simplicity in what you aim at, purity in what you love, the pair that lifts a person toward God, with every creature a page. The line was two wings.

Second place sounds like losing. So a phrase like love Jesus above all can land badly with the people we love most: a best friend, a partner, a kid. Wait, so I'm fourth? Some readers wrestle with chapter seven of book two of the Imitation for exactly that reason. It's short, it's intense, and the whole thing turns on one sentence: love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself. Two readings of it pull in different directions. Both deserve a hearing.
screen: `SECOND PLACE SOUNDS LIKE LOSING.` → `WAIT, SO I'M FOURTH?` → `TWO READINGS OF ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the case that the chapter is hard on human love. It says the love of creatures is deceitful and unstable, and whoever clings to a creature falls with the falling thing. Don't lean on a reed shaken by the wind, it warns, because all flesh is grass, a phrase it borrows from Isaiah. Some readers hear a monk's caution in that, written for men who had left home, and say ordinary life needs warmer words for a mother, a spouse, a friend. On that view, the chapter is true for the cloister and needs translating for the kitchen table. Now the case that the chapter is generous. Its key line doesn't say love Jesus instead of everyone. It says love all for Jesus, in Latin, propter Iesum, for his sake. On that reading nobody is demoted. Everyone else is loved through him, and he's loved for no reason beyond himself, so love for a friend doesn't fall when things fall. The chapter even promises a friend who won't leave when everyone else goes away. Catholic teaching holds the two commandments together: love God with your whole heart, and your neighbor as yourself. So both readings agree the friend matters, and both agree on the order. What they argue about is tone: whether the order should sound like a warning, or like a wider embrace.
screen: `CLING, AND YOU FALL WITH IT.` · `A MONK'S CAUTION?` · `LOVE ALL FOR JESUS.` · `LOVE GOD, LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · then, large: `ABOVE ALL, HOLDING THEM UP.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people you love, one by one, until you reach five or run out of fingers. Give each one a second of thanks as the finger goes down. If you pray, hold each one up to Jesus, for his sake. Either way, notice that you can love each one without gripping.
Loving Jesus above all. The Imitation's order of love: love everyone and everything for Jesus' sake, and Jesus for himself.
Pocket this one: above all, not instead of everyone else, but holding them all up. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of loving God above all as the first commandment, joined to love of neighbor, and some readers of the Imitation pray for the people they love by name, offering them to Christ.

notes: Imitation II.7 paraphrased: the love of the creature is deceitful and unstable, the love of Jesus faithful and enduring; he who cleaves to a creature falls with the falling; love him and keep him for your friend, who when all go away will not forsake you; love all for Jesus, but Jesus for himself; do not lean on a reed shaken by the wind, for all flesh is grass. Confirm each against the Latin.

Latin 'propter Iesum' is the phrase in 'Diligantur omnes propter Iesum, Iesus autem propter seipsum'. Confirm the wording and pronunciation (ecclesiastical). 'All flesh is grass' attributed to Isaiah 40:6; paraphrased.

v3 debate shape: two readings inside Catholic reading of the chapter (a monk's caution that needs warmer words for family life; a generous 'love all for Jesus' that demotes no one). Both are framed as 'some readers' / 'that reading'; neither is ranked. The great commandment (Matthew 22:37–39) is paraphrased as Catholic teaching.
